summary: A proposed Federal Information Processing Standard describing the format of messages passed between computer based message systems. Replaced by RFC 841.

plainLanguage.summary: Rules for how an electronic message should look so different mail systems can understand each other. A newer version replaced it.

questions: what fields must be in a message
how do different mail systems understand each other
what is the difference between message content and envelope
subtitle: A standard format for messages between different mail systems so they can understand each other.

tldr.problem: Different computer-based message systems could not exchange messages because they used different formats for message structure, fields, and data representation.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 806 defines a common format specifying which fields all messages must have (like From, To, and Posted-Date), what those fields mean, and how to encode the data so any compliant system can read messages from any other.
tldr.outcome: This was a proposed Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS), but was replaced by RFC 841 which incorporated feedback and refinements.

today: RFC 806 is a historic specification superseded by RFC 841. While no longer the active standard, its structured approach to message format specification influenced later work in email standards and message systems interoperability.

sections.title: The Problem of Message Incompatibility
sections.content:
Computer-based message systems (CBMSs) were becoming widespread in offices and research centers, but each system used its own format for messages. When users on different systems needed to send messages to each other, their systems could not understand the messages because they had different ideas about what fields should be in a message, what order they should appear in, and how to represent the data.

RFC 806 was developed as a proposed Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) to solve this problem. It specifies the form and meaning of messages that pass between different CBMSs, ensuring that systems from different vendors could exchange messages reliably.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine if every post office used a different layout for addresses. One might put the zip code first, another might put it last. Without a standard, mail could get lost. RFC 806 created the standard layout so all mail systems could work together.

sections.title: A Model for Message Systems
sections.content:
The specification describes how a CBMS works using a functional model with three main components. User Agents are the software that help people create and read messages. The Message Transfer System accepts messages from one person's User Agent and delivers them to another person's User Agent. These components communicate through two protocols: the Posting Protocol (from user to transfer system) and the Delivery Protocol (from transfer system to user).

A message has two parts: the message content (what the sender wanted to say) and the message envelope (information the transfer system needs to route it). The specification defines only the message content format, not the envelope or how it travels.
sections.plainLanguage: A CBMS works like a postal system: you write your message (the content), give it to the post office (the Message Transfer System), and they deliver it to the recipient. RFC 806 only specifies what the message itself looks like, not how the post office delivers it.

sections.title: Message Fields and Their Meanings
sections.content:
Every message is made up of fields, each serving a specific purpose. The specification organizes fields into six functional categories.

Originator fields identify who created and sent the message, such as the required From field and optional Author and Sender fields. Recipient fields say who should receive it, with the required To field for primary recipients and optional fields like Cc (carbon copies) and Bcc (blind carbon copies).

Date fields record when events happen: the required Posted-Date (when the message entered the transfer system), optional Received-Date (delivery time), and lifecycle dates like Start-Date and End-Date. Cross-reference fields link messages together using message identifiers and reply references. Message-handling fields specify how the message should be treated, such as precedence level. Message-content fields carry the actual information: a required Subject, required Text, and optional Attachments.

Fields are classified as REQUIRED (must appear in all messages), BASIC (should be processed when present), or OPTIONAL (may be ignored).
sections.plainLanguage: A message is like a postcard with different sections: one for who sent it, one for who receives it, one for the date, one for the message itself, and extra ones for special instructions. Different systems might use different sections, but when they exchange messages, both must understand what each section means.

sections.title: Data Encoding and Representation
sections.content:
Beyond the meaning of fields, messages must be represented in a consistent way so any system can parse and understand them. RFC 806 specifies the syntax, or encoding rules, for representing message fields and data elements.

The specification defines two types of data elements: primitives (like text strings, integers, or octal values) and constructors (complex types made up of primitives). Each data element has an identifier octet that indicates its type, followed by a length code, a qualifier if needed, and the actual data.

This encoding scheme allows messages to be compact while remaining extensible. The specification supports optional data compression and encryption identifiers, letting messages include encoded data. Messages can include vendor-defined extensions for functionality beyond the standard set, as long as the extensions do not duplicate functionality already covered by required, basic, or optional fields.
sections.plainLanguage: The syntax is like the rules for how to write an address on an envelope: city name, then state, then zip code, each in its own line, in a standard order. This way, any mail sorting machine can read it, even if the machine comes from a different company.

sections.title: What RFC 806 Does and Does Not Cover
sections.content:
The specification is focused and does not try to solve every problem. It specifies the form and meaning of message contents at the points when they are sent from one CBMS and received by another. It defines which fields must be present, which can be optional, how they should be represented, and what they mean.

However, RFC 806 explicitly does not specify the protocols used by the Message Transfer System, the format of message envelopes, how the transfer system routes messages, how CBMS applications should present messages to users, how messages are stored inside a CBMS, or how to identify message originators and recipients (the syntax and semantics of addressing are left to other standards).

This scope limitation makes the specification practical: different implementations can still innovate in areas outside the specification while remaining compatible for the interchange of messages.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 806 only specifies what the message looks like when it travels between systems. It does not say how systems should store messages, how users should read them on screen, or how the post office should deliver them. That is up to each system.

sections.title: Status and Legacy
sections.content:
RFC 806 was a proposed Federal Information Processing Standard issued in September 1981. It drew from existing CBMSs in both commercial and research environments, designed to be viable (using concepts that already worked), compatible (incorporating ideas from existing systems), and extensible (allowing both required fields and many optional ones, plus mechanisms for extensions).

The specification was superseded by RFC 841, which refined the approach and addressed feedback from implementation experience. Though RFC 806 is historic, its core concepts for message interchange remain relevant in modern email standards.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 806 was like the first draft of a rulebook for mail systems, written in 1981. A better version came out later (RFC 841), so RFC 806 was no longer the official standard. But the ideas in it were good and influenced later email standards.

items.title: Originator
items.text: Identifies who created and sent the message (From, Author, Sender).

items.title: Recipient
items.text: Specifies who receives the message (To, Cc, Bcc).

items.title: Date
items.text: Records when events happen (Posted-Date, Received-Date, Start-Date, End-Date).

items.title: Cross-reference
items.text: Links messages together using unique identifiers and reply references.

items.title: Message-handling
items.text: Describes how the message should be treated (precedence, class, reissue type).

items.title: Content
items.text: Carries the message information (Subject, Text, Attachments).
